{{Short description|Distance measure in statistics}}
In [[statistics]], '''Gower's distance''' between two mixed-type objects is a [[similarity measure]] that can handle different types of data (binary, ordinal, continuous) within the same dataset (unlike [[Hamming distance]] or [[Euclidean distance]]), by normalizing the differences between each pair of variables and then computing a weighted average of these differences.

The distance was defined in 1971 by Gower<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gower|first1=John C|date=1971|title=A general coefficient of similarity and some of its properties|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2528823|journal=Biometrics|volume=27|issue=4|pages=857–871|doi=10.2307/2528823 |jstor=2528823 |access-date=2024-06-03|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and it takes values between 0 and 1. This technique is particularly useful in [[cluster analysis]] (such as [[K-nearest neighbors algorithm]]) or other multivariate statistical techniques.

== Definition ==

For two objects <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> having  <math>p</math> descriptors, the similarity <math>S</math> is defined as:
<math display="block">S_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^pw_{ijk}s_{ijk}}{\sum_{k=1}^pw_{ijk}},</math>

where the <math>w_{ijk}</math> are non-negative weights usually set to <math>1</math> <ref>{{cite book |last1=Borg |first1=Ingwer |last2=Groenen |first2=Patrick J. F. |title=Modern multidimensional scaling: theory and applications |date=2005 |publisher=Springer |location=New York [Heidelberg] |isbn=978-0387-25150-9 |pages=124–125 |edition=2}}</ref> and <math>s_{ijk}</math> is the similarity between the two objects regarding their  <math>k</math>-th variable. If the variable is binary or ordinal, the values of <math>s_{ijk}</math> are 0 or 1, with 1 denoting equality. If the variable is continuous,  <math>s_{ijk} = 1- \frac{|x_i-x_j|}{R_k}</math> with <math>R_k</math> being the range of <math>k</math>-th variable and thus ensuring <math>0\leq s_{ijk}\leq 1</math>. As a result, the overall similarity <math>S_{ij}</math> between two objects is the weighted average of the
similarities calculated for all their descriptors.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Legendre |first1=Pierre |last2=Legendre |first2=Louis |title=Numerical ecology |date=2012 |publisher=Elsevier |location=Amsterdam |isbn=978-0-444-53868-0 |pages=278–280 |edition=Third English}}</ref>

In its original exposition, the distance does not treat ordinal variables in a special manner. In the 1990s, first Kaufman and [[Peter Rousseeuw|Rousseeuw]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kaufman |first1=Leonard |last2=Rousseeuw |first2=Peter J. |title=Finding groups in data: an introduction to cluster analysis |date=1990|pages=35–36 |publisher=Wiley |location=New York |isbn=9780471878766}}</ref> and later Podani<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Podani |first1=János |title=Extending Gower's general coefficient of similarity to ordinal characters |journal=Taxon |date=May 1999 |jstor=1224438|volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=331–340|doi=10.2307/1224438 |bibcode=1999Taxon..48..331P }}</ref> suggested extensions where the ordering of an ordinal feature is used. For example, Podani obtains relative rank differences as <math>s_{ijk} = 1- \frac{|r_i-r_j|}{\max{\{r\}}- \min{\{r\}}}</math> with <math>r</math> being the ranks corresponding to the ordered categories of the <math>k</math>-th variable.
